passage: Coach's note, Tuesday. After the inter-school semifinal, Nitin threw his bag across the changing room and told the team, "I'm never passing to Kabir again. Never. I'm done with him." His jaw was tight and his voice shook. Kabir stood by the door looking down. I did not argue with the vow. I sat by Nitin and said, "That sounds like a lot to carry tonight. Do you want to make that promise tomorrow, when the match isn't still in your chest?" Nitin frowned but nodded. On Wednesday he told me the pass had been Kabir's mistake, and that he still wanted to play with him, though he was still annoyed. Varun, coach.

qa.q: What did Nitin throw across the changing room?
qa.a: He threw his bag across the changing room.

qa.q: What did Nitin's vow suggest he was feeling?
qa.a: He was probably angry and disappointed about losing the semifinal, since his jaw was tight and his voice shook. The vow may not reflect what he wants once the feeling settles.

qa.q: What did the coach do that worked?
qa.a: Varun did not argue with the vow, acknowledged the heaviness and suggested waiting until the next day to decide.

qa.q: How might Kabir have felt while standing by the door?
qa.a: He may have felt hurt and guilty, which could be why he kept looking down.

grounding: A teenager vows under strong emotion, and waiting a day lets the intention settle.

Saturday, 9:15 pm

Chetan here, writing angry. I wrote on my hand in pen: never talk to Leela again. She told everyone in the group I was scared of the dark, and they all laughed. My face was burning. I swore I would delete her number, ignore her at school and stop going to the terrace where we hang out.

But Dadi looked at my hand and said, "Beta, that's a big promise for a Saturday night. Decide on Monday." I rolled my eyes.

Monday, 8 am: I washed my hand. I still don't want to talk to her today, but forever feels different. I think I just want her to say sorry. 🙁

qa.a: Chetan felt embarrassed and hurt, and by Monday realised that what Chetan mostly wants is an apology from Leela. The burning face on Saturday shows the strength of the moment.

passage:
The maths result came out on Tuesday, pinned outside the headmaster's room of the kasba school. Saurabh had failed by four marks.
He walked home kicking every stone. At the gate he announced to his older brother, Pankaj, who was fixing the tube well pump: "From tomorrow, I'm quitting cricket forever. Fourteen hours of study a day. No TV, no friends. I swear."
Pankaj wiped his oily hands. "Fourteen hours? You sleep ten."
"I'm serious!"
"I know. So stay serious till tomorrow evening. Then tell me the plan again."
Saurabh stomped inside.
On Wednesday evening he came out with a notebook page. "One hour maths every day after school. Cricket on Sundays only, till the retest."
Pankaj read it and nodded. "That one," he said, "you'll actually do."

qa.q: By how many marks did Saurabh fail?
qa.a: Saurabh had failed by four marks.

qa.q: What was Saurabh feeling when he swore to quit cricket forever?
qa.a: He was upset, ashamed and angry with himself after failing, and the huge vow was that feeling talking.

qa.q: Why did Pankaj's response work?
qa.a: By asking Saurabh to stay serious until the next evening instead of mocking or accepting the vow, Pankaj let the emotion settle so a realistic plan could come out.

qa.q: How might Pankaj have seen the first vow?
qa.a: Pankaj probably saw it as a burst of disappointment that would not last, which is why he gently tested it rather than taking it at face value.

grounding: The scene shows a teenager vowing a total change under strong emotion, and waiting a day turning it into a real intention.

passage:
In Kraków, the school concert ended at eight. Marek played his cello solo to a hall where the third seat in the second row stayed empty. His father had promised to come straight from work.
On the tram home, Marek told his friend Kaito, "I'm done with him. I'm never speaking to him again. Never."
Kaito looked at him. "That sounds really painful."
"It is. And I mean it."
"Okay. Will you still mean it tomorrow?"
Marek stared out at the lit shops and didn't answer.
Next morning, his father was waiting in the kitchen, grey-faced. His train had been stopped for three hours, his phone dead. He had the programme from the concert website printed out, with Marek's name circled.
Marek was still angry. But he sat down. "You can hear the recording," he said. "If you want."

qa.q: How long had his father's train been stopped?
qa.a: His father's train had been stopped for three hours.

qa.q: What was Marek feeling on the tram when he vowed never to speak to his father again?
qa.a: He was deeply hurt and angry that the seat stayed empty during his solo, and the pain made the vow feel certain.

qa.q: How did Kaito help without arguing?
qa.a: Kaito named the pain and then asked if Marek would still mean it tomorrow, which planted the idea of waiting before a big vow.

qa.q: What was it like for Marek's father to miss the concert?
qa.a: He seems to have felt awful and helpless, stuck on a train with a dead phone, and he showed he cared by circling Marek's name on the programme.

grounding: The scene shows a teenager vowing in anger never to speak to his father, and waiting a day letting his real intention settle.

passage: The final whistle went at the district sports club, and the scoreboard still read 0–3. Imran yanked off his bib and flung it at the bench. "That's it. I'm quitting. I'm never playing with this team again, I swear." His voice cracked on the last word. A few juniors froze mid-sip. Coach Uma didn't argue. She picked up the bib, folded it and held it out. "You can quit. Just not tonight. Tonight you're too angry to hear yourself. Come to the ground tomorrow after breakfast and tell me then." Imran snatched the bib and stomped to the bus. Next morning he turned up in slippers, hands in his pockets. "I don't want to quit," he mumbled. "I want to stop being played at left back when I'm a striker." Coach Uma nodded slowly. "That, we can talk about."

qa.q: What did the scoreboard read at the final whistle?
qa.a: The scoreboard still read 0–3.

qa.q: What does Imran's cracking voice suggest he was feeling?
qa.a: Imran was angry and deeply disappointed, and possibly ashamed of the loss; the vow came from that rush of feeling rather than a settled decision.

qa.q: Why was Coach Uma's 'just not tonight' a wise response?
qa.a: She neither argued nor accepted the vow but gave it a night to settle, and next morning the real wish came out: to play as a striker.

qa.q: How might the juniors who froze have seen the outburst?
qa.a: They may have been startled and unsure whether an older player was really leaving, which shows how a public vow made in anger unsettles others too.

grounding: It shows a teenager swearing to quit in a burst of anger and a coach suggesting a night's wait, after which the real intention comes out.
